utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, on the 11th of February 2009, I would like to greet the accused, Defence teams, the OTP, and Mr. Stringer and all his associates. And I wouldn't like to forget everyone else assisting us in these proceedings. The Registry, the usher, and the interpreters. I'll give the floor to the Registrar to deal with some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted list of documents to be tendered through witness Slobodan Bozic. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 00913. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC 00914. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC 00915. And the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 00916. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like us to move into closed session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As the court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, as you can see -- well, you said that there was an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honour, I haven't heard and I haven't seen in the transcript that IC list submitted by Mr. Praljak was given IC number. It might be mistake but I'm sure that we sent it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be best if the Registrar repeated the four numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through witness Slobodan Bozic. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 913. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC 914. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC 915. And the list submitted by Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 916. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Awfully sorry, but we submitted two lists, one -- okay, yes. I'm just given the sign. It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Could you give me your first and last name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. My name is Stipo Buljan. I was born in 1960 in Kuljanovci in the municipality of Derventa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But on what day, which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 2nd of January, 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I work as a functionary, and I work as a secretary in the ministry, Ministry of Energy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before Tribunal with regard to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have never testified before. This is the first time before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read the solemn declaration out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to provide you with some information to ensure that the proceedings run smoothly. As Mr. Stojic's counsel has certainly told you, you will have to answer questions that will be put to you on the basis of certain documents. This was certainly explained to you in detail. Once this has been done, the Prosecution will conduct its cross-examination, but before they do so the other Defence teams for representing the other accused may put questions to you as part of their cross-examination. The four judges sitting before you may, as a rule on base of documents, ask you to provide additional information or clarification. So we should be sitting or your testimony should take two days. We'll be sitting tomorrow -- you'll be testifying tomorrow, you'll see that it's quite exhausting because you have to remain concentrated to answer the questions. If you don't understand the sense of a question, please don't hesitate to ask the party putting the question to you to repeat it. You'll see that the type of questions put to you are quite different. Stojic Defence will put questions to you that will allow you to enlarge on the subject. In the course of the cross-examination, the Prosecution's questions will be questions to which you can answer by saying yes, no, I don't know, or perhaps. The other Defence teams will put questions to you, the nature of which will be somewhat hybrid. The Judges have a totally different approach because their questions are usually of a technical kind. They are open-ended questions that allow the witness a certain latitude when answering the questions. We'll have a break every one and a half hours. If at any point in time you feel somewhat uneasy, inform us of the fact, and we can adjourn. You are now testifying for the Court, which means that you should no longer have any contact with Ms. Nozica, that's especially the case now. You shouldn't have any more contact. That's what I wanted to tell you so that things can run smoothly. Ms. Nozica, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I would like to wish good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom and greet you, Mr. Buljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have provided some basic information about yourself to His Honour. Now, could you please in order to avoid more questions and to cover these rather important issues quickly, could you tell Their Honours and give them an explanation about the basic points of your career from your secondary school education up to the present. What were the activities you engaged in as your CV.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I said when I was born and where. I completed secondary technical school in Derventa. The mechanical engineering factory in Sarajevo. I enrolled in post-graduate studies in 1998, 1999 in Mostar. I defended my masters thesis in 2001 at the faculty of machine building in Mostar. I defended my PhD in 2007 at the faculty of machine building in Mostar, and last year I was promoted to the level of dosant [phoen] at the faculty of mechanical engineering in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you could speak a little more slowly. You are giving dates and for everything to be recorded in the transcript, please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Upon the completion of my university training, my first employment was in the work organisation practice of Orasje in the basic organisation for cold, processing of material. This was a firm engaging in the military industry. After that I moved to Derventa to a wonderful company which was called Mehanika, and it had 480 employees. I was head of production in that company when the war broke out. And in April 1992, I joined the Croatian Defence Council. During those first few months I was a soldier on the frontline, and after that assistant commander for IPD, and after that acting commander of the 103rd Derventa Brigade, and after that I was appointed to chief of the department attached to the operative zone Orasje in Bosanska Posavina, and I performed those duties until 1995 when I was appointed head of the administration for welfare. After that, by decision of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was appointed deputy director in the federal administration for veterans and fighters of the homeland war. I worked there for two years. After that, appointed to deputy director for the administration for civil defence. And in 2002 by decision of the government of BiH, I was appointed to the federal ministry for industry. And this is the post I hold today.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I note that quite a number of data that you mentioned have not been recorded. We see the letter D when you said Derventa, but for Their Honours to be able to have full insight in the period that is important for us I will ask you to go back to it. You said that you joined the HVO in April 1992 in Derventa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that at the beginning you were a foot soldier and that after a while you were assistant commander for IPD in the 103rd Brigade

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And after that acting commander of the brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you said that in April 1993, you were appointed chief of the department for welfare in the operative zone of Bosanska Posavina, Bosanska Posavina, and you held that position until 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, I've already told you that, but let me remind you, we will make brief pauses between questions and answers so that everything can be recorded in the transcript. Could you now please explain to Their Honours after you joined the HVO of Derventa, what was going on in Derventa, but I ask you to explain to Their Honours in geographical terms the location of Derventa.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In April 1992 when I joined the HVO, the frontline of the 103rd Derventa Brigade was very long. Derventa is a small town, a town of a municipality of 56.000 inhabitants, is in Bosanska Posavina, therefore, close to Bosanski Brod and Slavinski Brod. Also in Derventa municipality there were 52 villages and at that point in time the frontline was more than 100 kilometres long. Towards the end of April and the beginning of May the civilian authorities were moved out of Derventa municipality. They were somewhere else. The brigade remained alone there, and throughout those first two months, I was deployed on the frontline. Throughout the period that we are talking about, the 103rd Derventa Brigade was losing territory from a stronger enemy, and in a sense, it was retreating. On the 4th of July, 1992, the town of Derventa actually fell. That morning there was no one left in that town. My brigade formed a line not far from the town of Derventa between Bosanski Brod and Derventa and engaged in battle again, and later towards the end of September, or to be more precise, on the 6th of October, 1992, Bosanski Brod fell, the last square metres of Derventa municipality, and there wasn't a single unit of the HVO left in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, when you speak of a stronger enemy, to make it quite precise for the record, who was the enemy and who was attacking throughout this period that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I would define that as the Serbian army. The 103rd Derventa Brigade was waging war exclusively with the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have told us what happened to your brigade. Could you tell us now what was happening to the other HVO brigades from this area?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: At that point in time on the 5th of October, 1992, and the 6th of October, 1992, my brigade was to the right of Bosanski Brod, and the manpower was in the brigade. Under the attacks of the Serbian army, Bosanski Brod fell. And the 103rd Derventa Brigade with a few more units of the HVO was the only one left within that horseshoe. As it was realised that nothing could be done, the Sava river was behind us and the retreat was carried out across the Sava river, and the 103rd Derventa Brigade was stationed in schools in Slavonski Brod, in empty homes, houses, and the command of the brigade was in Orasje close to Slavonski Brod. That is where the brigade stayed for about a month. It was training there, and then it returned to Bosanski Posavina to a locality called Orasje, or, rather, Domaljevac close to Orasje. The 101st Brigade of Bosanski Brod went through the same events, and it also returned to Orasje afterwards. A little earlier on because the municipality of Modrica and Odzak had fallen earlier, those brigades too moved to the territory of free Slobodana [as interpreted] Posavina, that is in Orasje and the surrounding localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see that the place called Orasje does not appear in the transcript once though you referred to it several times, O-r-a-s-j-e. There's no problem. I'll repeat this later on to help you, but could you now mention the place where your 103rd Brigade was relocated?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: It's called Domaljevac which is close to Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, could you please list by name all the brigades that were where the 103rd Derventa Brigade was. You said this was roughly in mid-October. Which other brigades were stationed there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: One might say that in mid-November, or that is when we arrived there, we found the following situation: 101st Bosanski Brod Brigade, 102nd Odzak Brigade, 103rd Derventa Brigade, 104th Samac or Domicile Brigade, the 105th Modrica Brigade, and 106th Orasje Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that the 103rd Derventa Brigade was in conflict with the Serbian army. Tell us what operative zones were constituted by these brigades, and who they were fighting throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: These brigades constituted the operative zone of Bosanska Posavina, and all these brigades throughout the war were in conflict and fighting the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have seen when the war started. Could you tell us up until when did this war continue?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The last more serious and strong offensive was around June or July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the area of Orasje, that is within the territory of the operative zone of Bosanska Posavina, were there any units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, there were no units of the armija there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell me what was the ethnic composition of these HVO brigades?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I can say that each of these six brigades was multiethnic in composition. The 101st Bosanski Brod Brigade had a significant number of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity and also of Serb ethnicity and others, as well as the command personnel of the said brigade. The same applied to the 102nd Odzak Brigade. I think that the Chief of Staff there was a Muslim, and the assistant commander for IPD was also a Muslim. In the 103rd Derventa Brigade, that is my brigade, there were also quite a number of Muslims. The chief of the medical corps was also a Muslim. In the 104th Samac Brigade there were also other ethnicities. In the 105th Modrica and 106th Orasje Brigades there were both soldiers and command staff who were of various ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me please, in the command of the operative zone, was it of mixed ethnicity, I'm talking about the command?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, the command of the operative zone was also of mixed ethnicity. I think that the main intelligence officer in the zone was a Bosniak, and there were other operative officers who were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell me, Mr. Buljan, what were the insignia worn by HVO soldiers from April 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: One could say that the markings were such that there was an indication of the HVO, but also an indication of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This applied in particular to the Muslims who wore such markings, so a kind of mixture was produced. Half was HVO and the other half were three lilies. And this went on until perhaps the end of 1992 and even the beginning of 1993. The brigade took a long time to organise itself, and I remember the 102nd Odzak Brigade and the commander Bozic had this until mid-1993. Later on as the HVO organised itself, such insignia were gradually removed and only the insignia of the HVO were borne. The removal of these mixed insignia or double insignias, sometimes both were worn on the coat, this went gradually and it was not by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please explain something. When you said "mixed" badges, could you tell us what kind of badges they were? Did you have two insignia on one badge or was it on one shoulder? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, often you would have two kinds of insignia, two badges, they would be separate, distinct on the uniforms. But sometimes the HVO insignia would be split in half and you would have half the insignia of the ABiH and the other half of the HVO insignia, and then you'd have just one badge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did the Muslims from October 1992 and onwards leave HVO units? Was this a large scale phenomenon, what could you say about this?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Given the situation we were in, especially the brigades that had lost their territory, the 102nd, the 103rd, the 101st, and the 105th, well, given the situation, there were soldiers who left. I also remember in 1992 in October after the fall of Bosanski Brod, after the bridge had been blown up, while we were billeted in Oreovac [phoen], there was one unit, perhaps a platoon or a strengthened platoon, and mainly the members of the platoon were Muslims. They and their equipment from the 103rd Derventa Brigade set off through Zagreb and arrived in Central Bosnia, perhaps in Zenica, and this movement of the armed soldiers hadn't been something that we were informed of. Some of those people returned to Orasje. But -- however, there were some that got through and everything came to an end, I would sometimes -- when everything was over I would sometimes meet them in Zenica, but they went to the central part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the following period during the entire wartime period, in that area up until 1995, as you said, were there a lot of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity who left? Was this a large scale phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, no, I can't say that there were more Muslims who left than Croats or members of other ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that at the beginning of April 1992 when you joined the HVO you were assistant commander for IPD, intelligence and propaganda. For how long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I held that position for perhaps two or three months. I can't say exactly now, but it was after the fall of Derventa, the fall of the municipality or town of Derventa, the 103rd Derventa Brigade was in Bosanski Brod at the time. In such situations usually the command staff when the territory is left, disappears, and then the command of the 103rd Derventa Brigade appointed me to this position and assigned specific tasks to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Similarly, you said that you were the acting brigade commander. When was this? I just wanted to add, so that we have a complete answer, I wanted to ask you what happened to the commander?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This was from about the beginning of November, the first ten days of November, 1992, until perhaps the end of January, 1993. The brigade commander was seriously wounded in fighting in Bosanski Brod. He was in hospital, and they appointed me to that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who was in the command of the brigade you were in?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, on the whole there were -- there was the assistant for IPD, there was the chief of security, the chief of logistics, the chief of sanitation and health, so that's how the brigade was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were they all your assistants?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, they were practically all my assistants. They were the first individuals in those fields who were members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the command structure in the operation zone was like, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, it was similar, almost an identical reflection of what a brigade usually is like. That's what the situation was like in the operation zone. There was a commander of the operation zone, there was a chief of the staff of the zone in question, there was an assistant for IPD, there was an assistant for security; I think that that was the name. There was an assistant for intelligence and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll go back to the subject of your brigade. Can you explain for the benefit of the Chamber to whom assistance for IPD, security, sanitation, logistics were subordinate? Who were they subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The time and situation that prevailed during that wartime period, they were subordinate to me alone. Every morning assigned task to them, I told them what they should do, how they should do it, and how they should report on what they were doing me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what the link was between these assistants and assistants from the same fields in the operations areas?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, I think they had certain meetings, certain information was gathered on such occasions, so someone from the operation zone could inform commander of the operation zone about the issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, you said at that time, that was the period during which you held that position. It was from November 1992 until the end of January or the beginning of February 1993, I'm only asking you about that period because that's the experience you have. Now, my question is, what was the relationship of your assistants for IPD, security, sanitation and logistics in your brigade with the fields, with the sectors in those fields in the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way, my own assistants for my brigade worked with the assistant of the general area in relation to certain fields and sectors. And then the assistants for certain areas was in charge of some form of coordination and in charge of making sure there were appropriate links to assistants in the departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just to make sure the Chamber understands, at the time were there any physical links that were available to you for your communication with, for example, Herzegovina? What was the actual communication like in terms of technology and in terms of physical links to Herzegovina and Mostar specifically? I'm talking about the period between November 1992 and onward from there.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This was still a time when it was very difficult to communicate. Even to just travel there required a long time. You had to cross Croatia in its entirety in order to reach Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about communications? I'm now talking about the actual technology, the equipment used. Do you remember if the military were using anything to communicate on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't think there was any such thing as daily communication going on, but at any rate communication was possible by phone if nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, I'm taking account of a single detail so don't hold this against me when you tell me you had to cross Croatia in its entirety. Can you tell Your Honours if there was a short cut that one could take in order to get to Mostar and why that short cut could not be used at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Bosanski Posavina and this whole area around Orasje had the Sava river right behind it. It was broad and it was cold and in front there was a 27 kilometre long front with the enemy all over it. The only way to cross this area was by air, across Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to get to Herzegovina proper. So everyone travelled across the Republic of Croatia, along the Adriatic coast and across the islands back to the mainland before one could make the crossing into Herzegovina or Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In order to explain why one had to cross a portion of the sea and across the islands, can you please explain that. Was perhaps a section of the Croatian coast occupied as well and by whom?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: That's right, a section of the coast belonging to the Republic of Croatia was at the time occupied by the Serb army, and one couldn't cross that section. One would have to take a ferry to circumvent this section and in order to return to the free territory of the Republic of Croatia, and I think planes were used for travel at the time in order to cross that area as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, you say that throughout this time up until 1995 it was only the Serbian army that you waged war against. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber about this Serbian army. Aside from the areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina which you explained you were holding under your control, were there any combat activities or operations that they were performing across your territory in order to jeopardize the Republic of Croatia, to attack the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: While we were still in the Bosanski Brod area, I do have to admit that it was equally dangerous to be in Slavonski Brod or further behind Bosanski Brod's territory. I can't be specific, but I think the shelling of Zupanja lasted over 1.000 days. Before the frontline eventually moved to Bosanska Posavina and the area Orasje. Long range artillery was used by the Serbian army to pound our own frontline and deeper into our territory as well as the fringe areas including certain towns in the Republic of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please go back to the structure of your own brigade. At the time was there anyone in the brigade who was in charge of welfare?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, I have to admit not. In the 103rd Derventa Brigade there was no particular person at a time who was in charge of welfare, and the same thing applied across the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just, you know, to make sure we make this clear, what period of time are we looking at? When was there no one who was in charge of welfare?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about persons whose sole responsibility it was to look after welfare. There was no one throughout 1992 in the units of the Croatian Defence Council in Bosanska Posavina. It wasn't before the beginning of 1993 that an appointment like that was first made and the post was filled, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you the person appointed, Mr. Buljan, appointed to any post that had to do with welfare within the operation zone, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: It was in March 1993 that I was appointed head of the welfare section in the Bosanska Posavina operations area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Who signed your appointment?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: My appointment was signed by the head of that department, Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there a person in each brigade who was in charge of welfare at the time, or by this time? I'm talking about the period that followed April 1993.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Once I had been appointed, I carried out additional consultations with my erstwhile colleagues, brigade commanders. I also talked to the commander of the operations area and asked him to do the same. I said that there should be an appointment, that people should be appointed within a ten-day period who would be in charge of welfare across the units. In some units there was a single person who was in charge. In some others there were a number of different persons who dealt with this area. For the most part all the commanders complied with this. Following which, each of the brigades had a person was in charge of welfare and some sort of link between the brigade and the welfare section or department in the operations area itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, can you explain to the Court what sort of relationship existed between you and the commander of the operation zone or area in terms of welfare now that you've assumed your post, and what was the relationship between you and the head of welfare and the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I had my own commander, the commander of the operations area, and I was responsibility to the commander directly for all areas. I was not for a moment allowed to leave the area or do anything else without his written or verbal permission. I was the department head and I was in charge of welfare. We sometimes spoke, we exchanged information, I would submit certain reports when required and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When, based on what you remember, did the welfare administration that was attached to the Defence Department start operating?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I think it was sometime mid-through 1993, perhaps May or June.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you remember what the name was of the head of the welfare administration within the Defence Department at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Sure. Josip Palac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, we'll be going through a number of exhibits now, if you don't mind, to support what you've been telling us. I assume you've been given a binder containing documents. Do you have that in front of you, sir? It should be a blue binder. That's the one, yes. The first document, we'll take one step at a time, I'll try not to skip a single document. Can you please track down the first one for the sake of the record. This is 2D 00629. Tell me as soon as you've got it, sir.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I've found the document. This is the document in which we see the department head, Mr. Stojic make my official appointment as chief of the welfare section within the Bosanska Posavina operations area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said a minute ago that this was in March, whereas the date we see here is the 3rd of April, would that be the same thing, sir?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. It's probably down to me. I've probably got the date and the months mixed up. I think this should be accurate because this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please move on to the next document. This is 2D 00567. There will be a yellow sticky attached to that particular sheet of paper and you shouldn't find it too difficult to find document. This is decision on the internal structure of the Defence Department dated October 1992. I believe you saw the one from October 1992. Can you therefore tell the Court if you look at this first internal structure, was there such a thing envisaged there as a post relating to welfare or the head of a welfare section, anything like that at all?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, nothing like that that is contained in this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next document, please, this is P 02477. P, P, just for the sake of the record, sir. P 02477. This is a decision on the internal structure dated the 20th of May, 1993. Can you please focus on paragraph 2, rather item 2, paragraph 2 of item 2. You see that in May, just as you told us there was now such a thing as welfare administration and that had just been introduced right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document claims that heads will be in charge of the administration?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And they will answer to the deputy head. Do you remember who the deputy head was at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I do have to admit that all of my communication between myself and the welfare administration and any -- and the welfare administration itself went through Mr. Palac the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please move to the next document, please, 2D 01370. 2D 01370. That's the one. Have you got it, sir?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a diagram showing how the brigade was formed. We should have there a list of all of the duties incumbent upon the command of a brigade. Can you please go to page 3 of that document, sir. And there you should find appointments. Item 4, which should be the next page, as long as we get that in e-court. All right. We've got it. We have it on our screens. Go to number 4, please. It reads: "Coordinator for social welfare and care of the wounded." Is this a position that existed in the brigades based on what you remember?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. These for the most parts were the positions that formed a link between the brigade on the one hand and me and my colleagues in the welfare administrations across the operations areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please now go to P 02945. This is an order, an appointment being made to the Rama Brigade command. The order was signed by Bruno Stojic, head of the Defence Department. The date is the 25th of June, 1993. Can we just make sure whether the appointment was actually made. Look at number 20, please. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just to make sure we've got it in the transcript and in no uncertain terms, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Number 20, the person being appointed here is actually a social welfare clerk or coordinator, depending on the term being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, can you explain to the Trial Chamber -- I keep talking about your position, the position that you were appointed to in April, the 3rd of April more specifically. The Bosanska Posavina operations area. You were appointed head of the welfare section. Can you tell us if you were the person who drafted reports there? Did you draft any reports and for whose sake? What exactly did those reports comprise?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Welfare sections, that is myself and anyone else working there, would draft reports or produce reports. We would then forward those reports to the welfare administration. Their form and their substance was exactly what was required. Other such reports when needed would be sent on to the commander of the operations area as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps I misheard or misunderstood. These reports, did you submit these to the welfare administration in Mostar as well?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we move on to two of the following documents shedding light on this. The first is P 4699. Mr. Buljan, this is a work in progress report in relation to June and July 1993, HVO HZ-HB. I'm deliberately showing you none of the reports in relation to 1992 because we know when you were appointed when you first started working in this position. Can you please look at page 14 in the Croatian which should be page 9 in the English. If you look at the bottom of page 14 in the Croatian, you will see the beginning of a report on the tasks of the welfare administration. It then spills over in to page 15 and part of page 16. Can you in the briefest of terms tell the Chamber whether this information -- I believe you've gone through this carefully, whether all of this information contained in this report tallies with the information that you would include in your own annual reports?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, the information tallies. It's exactly consistent with information forwarded by my own section to the welfare administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please move on briefly to the next report also, P 07419. And then we can go into more detail with what exactly your job entailed. P 7419. This is a report on the work of the HVO in relation to the period between June and December 1993. Page 4 in the Croatian and page 2 in the English. This document talks about the sector for personnel affairs and within that sector about the department for welfare, and there's a detail link to you when it says that in December 1993 the department for welfare was established in Orasje and preparations were carried out to deal and to provide care for the wounded members of the HVO. Do you remember that in December 1993 the welfare department attached to the HVO were visited in the zone of Orasje?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that the employees of the administration for welfare did make a tour of the Welfare Department of the HVO in the territory of Orasje. It is true that 63, and I have no reason to doubt this number, that financial aid was paid out to families of the killed and war veterans wounded, and I would have left out the word "establishment" because it was a established by my appointment. As soon as I was appointed, the department was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. After your appointment as a chief of the department for welfare in the operative zone of Bosanska Posavina, what were your initial tasks?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: When I'm talking about welfare, then I'd divide that into two important segments. One, while I was chief of the sector or department in Orasje, and the second section when I was the head of the administration. When I took over as head of the sector in the operation zone of Bosanska Posavina, there was virtually nothing there so I started from scratch, and I received from the commander a room with a kitchen table, and I said from now on this will be my office. And this is where we collected data about all the victims. And we agreed on how we would collect data and provide those data to the department. So in the first place we had to identify the people involved. We had to send them for treatment if necessary, to engage in their rehabilitation, and in the case of all military invalids, this was essential. Also we needed to find orthopaedic aids for them, and in the case of those military war disabled who were unable to return to their homes, or rather who had nowhere to go, we had to find accommodation for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When talking about the first stage or the first period of your activities, you are now explaining the first period. You just didn't tell us when this second period belongs, according to you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The second stage or period will be as long as the first because it also started in April, but in 1995 in April or May when I was appointed head of the welfare administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So in this first stage you first collected data about those killed and those wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who collected those data? Were they collected in the brigades or at the level of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The only providers of information were the coordinators who were located in the brigades. Some brigades had several coordinators, some battalions of brigades had their own coordinators. It all depended on the size of the brigade. So they were the first persons to provide us with the requested information. It was up to me to decide how to organise this data. If we needed something to be signed by the brigade commanders, then those certificates which the brigade commanders needed to sign, they had to be equal, uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, while you were collecting these data, did you at the same time provide care to the war invalids and the families of the victims and how?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Certainly we did take care of all war invalids who, with necessary documents, received salaries through their original units, the unit in which they were wounded. Also, through our department they were provided with treatment, as I mentioned a moment ago. They were sent to various institutions for surgery or for orthopaedic aids, et cetera. This applied to the invalids, to the war disabled.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you take care of the families of the killed too?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The families of killed soldiers also were taken care of. We needed to do the same as for the war disabled with respect to documents. We needed to find out who was entitled to any fees after the death of a soldier, so that was our priority in the first period, to collect the necessary data.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you explain, Mr. Buljan, to the Trial Chamber, you have explained where you were in a territory that was jeopardized on the one side by the Serb army, and on the other behind you was the Sava river, where did you provide the treatment for members of your brigades who needed such treatment?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In the theatre of war of Orasje all the victims wounded were first put up in a wartime hospital which is close to Orasje, maybe a kilometre or two away from Orasje. The place is called Tolisa in a monastery. Half of the monastery was used a wartime hospital, and the other half of the Franciscan monastery was used for its original purpose. So we first had to see whether the wounds could be treated there, and if not then the closest larger hospital that we would send the war disabled to was in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could I correct the transcript. In line -- page 27, line 14, you mentioned the hospital of Tolisa.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said for the more difficult cases that they were sent to Slavonski Brod. Was Slavonski Brod in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. It is a small town on the Sava river across from Bosanski Brod. So it is close to the occupied territory of Bosanski Posavina. The aim was to remove the wounded and transport them across the river. There were no bridges there. The bridge had been blown up at the beginning of the war, so we used the ferries and boats to ferry them across the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we were speaking about the wounded, could you tell us whether the wartime disabled were provided with any rehabilitation or care after -- postoperative care, and where?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Every serious wound or surgical intervention, even lighter ones, required certain measure of rehabilitation, so that we sent our war disabled to Tolisa in Croatia through the department for welfare of Croatia. And when possible they went to Varazdinska [phoen] and Toplica [phoen], these are spas, Stublica [phoen], Toplica, again a spa for therocell [phoen] therapy and that kind of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At a later stage or you tell us when, did the war disabled go to motels in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: It was always a problem when all this was completed, that is his rehabilitation. If his house is somewhere in Modrica or Derventa or Bosanski Brod or Odzak, the question was where he could return to. He was a seriously disabled person and he had nowhere to go, and so we put such people up in certain hotels. One such was in Zenit in Krvavice [phoen], and later for the victims from Bosanska Posavina, again across the river from Orasje in Djakovo they were put up in an abandoned hotel, and this was a kind of centre where the war disabled could be accommodated after rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned the Zenit hotel. Where is this hotel?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The Zenit hotel is in Neum and Neum is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about treatment of war time invalids and their rehabilitation and care for the families of the killed, was any distinction made between Muslims and Croats who had either been killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: When providing welfare or assistance to the families of the wounded and the killed, and the missing, no distinction was made between them. The same care was provided for Croats, for Muslims, for a Serb who may have been in an HVO unit, or for other volunteers or foreign volunteers who may have been in HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, you said that the second stage of your activities started sometime in mid-1995. Could you explain what happened in this second stage. In the first we saw that you were collecting the basic data as to the killed and the wounded. What happened in the second stage?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In the first stage we collected the data that I indicated a moment ago. Also during that stage, that is up to 1995, the war disabled who had completed their rehabilitation were taken before first level commissions to establish the degree of disability. And this document was required for a subsequent process which was initiated towards the end of 2005 when I joined the welfare department, which led to the second level commissions when the percentage of their disability was established and assessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you tell me why did it take so long? Was it technically difficult not to engage in this activity immediately? How demanding was it for everything to be done until you reached the second level commission which established whether somebody was an invalid or a family member of a killed soldier?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: We wanted all documents to be uniform. There were files for the victims and these forms had to be filled in, collected, then first level commissions had to be formed who would express their findings and assessments regarding the degree of damage. The wartime invalids had to complete their treatment for their condition to be assessed and because of a shortage of manpower in the Defence Department who would carry out these activities, it wasn't until the end of 1995 that this entire process was completed and that there was a legal basis as stating that a certain person was a wartime invalid with such and such a degree of disability. Until then they were invalids but they didn't have this document certifying to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But we must not forget that throughout that period you did take care of them as far as you were able?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Certainly. Various ways were found to assist the wounded or the families of victims. Now, whether it involved extended rehabilitation, orthopaedic aids, or something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, could you tell us when this second stage, this legalisation stage started, and when it was completed? Was it ever completed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been completed to this day. This is a process that will take some more time to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have another ten minutes until the break. Could we look through some documents now linked to this part of your testimony. Would you look at document 2D 1245. That should be the next document in your binder after these reports. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, I'd prefer you to speak about the documents, tell us about the documents. Can you tell us what we are dealing with here and if I have any questions I'll put them to you. This is a three-page document and I'd like to go through it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This document shows that at the time referred to on the document, well, this first document is dated the 4th of August, 1993. This document shows that the brigade commander, the commander of the 101st Boski Brod Brigade, Zedjko [phoen] Barisic at the written request of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia informs that a certain person withdrew funds having been granted power of attorney, so this demonstrates how one proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, we can see that we are dealing with Smajo Mahmutovic. That's why we chose this example. You said that all individuals were taken care of regardless of the ethnicity. So the family of a HVO soldier from the 101st Brigade is concerned. If this soldier was killed, and it says that the authorised agent, Omar Carsovic no longer wishes to collect the salary, and they therefore request Mira, it's probably the wife or family member, they request her to inform the brigade who the new authorised agent will be. Don't speculate if you don't know the answer, but on the basis of his name, Mr. Smajo Mahmutovic, would you say this was a Muslim or Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Muslim, that is a Muslim name, so that's just one such example.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document -- the next page is a document authorizing someone providing power of attorney. Have a look at the third sheet, the third page, it mentions certain sums that were paid for this individual who was killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's a Bosanski Brod, 3rd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Buljan, have a look at the following document, 2D 00749. This is a decision on appointing medical commission in Mostar. It's signed by Bruno Stojic. The date is the 17th of March, 1993. It's a commission for military disabled in Mostar. We can see that there are certain doctors concerned, their names seem to indicate that they are Muslims. So could you comment on the document? I don't like to emphasise the fact that in the HVO, at the time there were both Croats and Muslims and there were some members of some other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on nominating a higher or, rather, second degree medical commission in Mostar, and you can see the composition of the medical commission. And the under number 2 you can see Dr. Ramo Omanovic, you can see that this is a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, you told us about the first part of your work, and then the second part that later involved implementing legal procedures to determine the invalidity status of given individuals and to determine how someone was killed, whether someone was a victim in the war, whether someone was a military invalid. So where would you place this decision on the nomination of a higher medical commission and this is what Mr. Stojic did in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, I think this decision preceded other decisions that were subsequently taken with regard to this second degree commission. But at the time that this decision was issued, it perhaps wasn't possible to act on the decision immediately because there was no infrastructure in place in all the Defence Departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at the following document, 2D 01246. That's the next document, and this is an order from Bruno Stojic again forwarded to the operations zones and to the Mostar HVO, Tomislavgrad-Orasje-Vitez, the Defence Department. This is September 1993. Please, could you tell the Court, is this one such attempt, is this an attempt made by Mr. Stojic to ensure that the legal aspects of this problem came into force?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was to be used by those who weren't willing to do what was requested in the order. So in a certain sense this is a new order in which people being requested to respect certain dead-lines with respect to providing means of work for people who were involved in welfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The people who were involved in welfare; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look at document 2D 01247. This is a decision signed by Mr. Stojic. The date is not really legible, but as you've already seen this document you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on appointing a department for the protection of municipalities. They will decide on the rights of veterans and of killed soldiers from areas temporarily occupied. The HR BH, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In such conditions, when someone loses their municipality, one acts differently. There aren't enough people, there aren't enough professionals, and then it's not possible to work. These were long term processes, procedures. You needed staff to be involved in these areas. You needed salaries for these people. Remuneration. This decision aided everyone who wasn't in their own territory, or in this order you can see who is responsible for drafting certain documents in relation to certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said individuals who weren't in their territory, because the territory was occupied, did that include you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. The territory of the Derventa municipality was completely under Serbian control from the 6th of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I would now like to move on to a more demanding document. I'd need a few minutes to deal with it, so would you rather we had a break now. I leave it to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you've used an hour and 20 minutes up, so you have another 40 minutes. We'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, let's please have a look at the following document, 2D 600626. You have it before you? Could you briefly tell the Chamber who drafted this document and could you tell us about the contents of the document. We have another 20 minutes, and I'd like you to comment on the other documents too. We have another 40 minutes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the welfare administration. I was the head of that administration. Five defence administrations were analysed, the total number of dead is shown, the number of those who died when they were salaried, the number of wounded is shown, the number of wounded involved in units, the number of wounded with salaries are shown, reasons for which certain individuals were salaried, the number of those missing and those missing with salaries. So this is a more detailed analysis. It's a report drafted by the welfare administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The date of this document is the 30th of November, 1996. Could you tell the Chamber whether this is the first time that such detailed information was obtained, and is this the result of the work that was carried out, as you said, in the second phase when conditions were in place to gather this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the result of that work. As I said, this is information that is a little more detailed. You have figures on the status of the casualties of the war invalids for whom there were certain decisions for compensation. There were certain decisions where the status of invalids was recognised. So these were some of the first reports that were drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before we move on it to documents that also show the ethnicity of the individuals and the number of the individuals killed and the number of war invalids and the brigades in your operation zone, before we do that could you look at 2D 00150. It's a separate document, the Judges also have a separate document. It's a report dated the 9th of June, 1996. And it's an analysis of the ethnicity of the individuals concerned. It's document 2D 00150. Yes, that's the one. Mr. Buljan, could you please comment on figures for the unit members that you are familiar with. It's on the second page, and these figures concern Muslims and Croats. On what basis were these figures provided, was this information provided, and can you confirm that this information is in fact correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at document from 1993 signed by the chief of the personnel department Jure Brkic. At the time he was the person authorised to sign such documents. And as far as the ethnicity of the members of the 101st, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6th brigade of the HVO, and they were in the Orasje battle-field, on that side of the corridor, as far as their ethnicity is concerned, well I think that what is shown here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Can we confirm once more that this document dated the 9th of June, 1993, that it is a document from 1993 and not from 1996, which is what it says on page 35, line 25. Mr. Buljan, let's have a look at the following document, 2D 00604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, this is an important document, and as you were from the 103rd Brigade you will certainly be able to answer my question. I wanted to ask you the following: In the month that this document was drafted in June 1993, at that time were you the acting commander of the 103rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in June 1993 I wasn't the acting commander of the 103rd Derventa Brigade, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Where were you in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June 1993, I was the chief of the welfare department in the Bosanska Posavina operations zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were in that operation zone. In the operation zone, there were HVO units in which there were Muslims too, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So do you know that in May 1993 there were certain events that took place in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you know that there were Muslims who were arrested or displaced or detained, let's say that they were taken from point A to point B, for some of them -- or some of them were taken to the Heliodrom, so we don't have to go into legal problems. Are you aware of that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not aware of that. Very well. And now for my last question which will be very simple. Given the events in May in Mostar, well, did these events have any repercussions with regard to the HVO units involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti asked you where you were at the time that these reports were forwarded, and you said that you were in the operation zone and you performed the duties you mentioned. Regardless of that position -- well, in the case of the 103rd Brigade, can you confirm that this information is correct because in spite of the fact that you were in the operation zone, you were in contact with the brigades that were part of that operation zone?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: If we are still dealing with the document from 1993, 2D 00150, and if we are talking about the six brigades that were in the Orasje battle-field, I can confirm and I do confirm that the ethnic composition -- well, was multiethnic, and I think that -- what you can see in the document reflects the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, can we now move on to another document, 2D 00604. Mr. Buljan, since the document mentions your name, could you briefly tell the Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, when I had certain information according to which I would be testifying before this Court, I asked the administration for those who were casualties in the homeland war, from the County Posavska, so that's the place where I worked and why I put this system into place, I asked that that office provide me with information. I asked them to provide me with information where everything was broken down on the base of people's ethnicity. I can see that the information is quite precise. Their first names, last names, name of father, and there is the identity, personal identity name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please go on to the next document, that's 2D 00605. We are now moving on to the set of documents, the lists that were submitted to you. Now, I would like to dwell a little longer on the first one in order to explain to the Chamber what the list means and how it's structured.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This list contains names of members of the HVO who were killed who hailed from Bosanski Brod municipality and these were ethnic Croats. This is the 101st Bosanski Brod Brigade, the HVO. This is a list containing all the names of the members who were killed. First name, last name, father's name, and personal identification number. The record is accurate and complete. Also, at the end of this document we see a reference here to the 106th Brigade [indiscernible] from Orasje and the Defence Ministry HR HB and the Derventa police administration is mentioned, too. Therefore, these lists were produced in such a way as to indicate all the information in relation to all the members from a given municipality regardless of where they came to grief, or what unit they were members of when they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the first list we see a total of 230 members who were ethnic Croats. This is a followed by a list of members of the HVO who were killed from Bosanski Brod municipality and these were ethnic Bosniaks; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. This was done in much the same way as the previous part of the list, the 101st Bosanski Brod Brigade were the ethnic Croats, so the next list was produced in relation to the same unit but it pertains to ethnic Bosniaks, or Muslims if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. The last page of this document in the Croatian version says, "Members of the HVO killed who are from Bosanski Brod municipality. Other ethnicities." Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. And this indicates that there were a total of 13 members of the 103rd Bosanski Brod who were killed who belonged to other ethnicities. They were neither Croats nor Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It might be better to go back to this first document and then we'll go on with a series of documents. There are a number of those and they are all structured in the same way. All these are members of the Croatian, Bosniak, and other ethnicities who were killed during clashes with which army? Can you be specific one more time, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The members of all these six units that I mentioned, the units that we are now talking about throughout the war were only ever clashing with the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, could you also tell me whether all these members that we are about to show, were taken care of in the way you described a minute ago, were looked after regardless of their ethnicity. We are talking about those killed. Were their families looked after, all equally regardless of their ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The families of all these persons who were killed were looked after in much the same way, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let's move quickly through the following documents 2D 00606, that is the next document that is up. The same kind of material but here we are dealing with members of the HVO Orasje municipality who were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It follows from this. This is the 106th Brigade of the HVO, Orasje, and the information was prepared in the same way as in relation to the previous unit that we dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you then please move on to 2D 00607.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The situation was this, the Bihac HVO was isolated within the Bihac pocket itself. They were alone and they belonged to no one in practical terms, so a number of people were killed who belonged to those units. It was easier for them to cross into Croatia and then reach Orasje via Croatia. It was decided that the welfare section of Orasje should take care of those who had been killed in the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now please move on to 2D 00608.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This is the 108 Brigade, the Brcko Brigade of the HVO. It was on the other side of the corridor across the Orasje frontline. The corridor ranged from somewhere near Brcko and then down the whole length of the line being held by the HVO and then further up towards Banja Luka. This unit was on the other side, the breadth of the corridor involved, we used to say, was within a decent firing range, that's what we used to say. So certain members went to the Republic of Croatia to receive treatment and for rehabilitation. So whenever this was the case, it was my department that would take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can we now please move on to 2D 00608. Oh, we just looked at that one. So this is 2D 00609.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This is the 103rd Brigade, the Derventa Brigade of the HVO, and all the information contained in this document was processed in much the same way as all the previous units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please move on to the next document then, 2D 006010 -- 610, in relation to Modrica. Can you explain this one please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The same sort of situation. Again, sometime midway through 1992, about July, Modrica fell. And all the soldiers from Modrica municipality crossed over into the Orasje theatre of war. So this was another brigade that was in our care.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is 2D 00611?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Everything that I said in relation to the previous document, the 105 Modrica Brigade, again this is a town that is adjacent to Modrica, this is Odzak, they are adjacent municipalities, and the same applies to Odzak. And the information was processed in much the same way in relation to Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's move on 2D 00612. This is a list of the members of the HVO who were killed in Tuzla municipality. Was Tuzla part of your operation zone, and can you please explain whether and why you looked after these members as well?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Again the 103 Tuzla Zrinski Brigade was very much alike of the previous ones. This one was adjacent to the 108 Brigade of the Croatian Defence Council from Brcko and we looked after it the same way as we did after the members of the 108 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you move please move on to the next document. This is 2D 00613. Here is a reference to a list of members killed in Gradacac municipality. Croats and other ethnicities as well.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. Again the 7th Brigade of the HVO, Gradacac, is the other side of the corridor. And all the members of the 107 Gradacac Brigade who, during the combat operations, left the zone, and if my department had access to them, were looked after the same way as long as they were in the Orasje area as all the other brigades that were on that side of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please move on to 2D 00614.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: These are the killed and wounded members of the 104 Brigade of the HVO Bosanska Samac. This brigade, for the most part -- well, was located in Domaljevac, the same place as my own brigade, and this information was processed in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just to be specific as possible, this is the a list of members who were killed, and we are only about to get to the wounded; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. You are entirely right, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now please move on to 2D 00615. This is a list of the invalids of war, HVO, Bihac municipality, Croats. And the document moves on to a list of war invalids, Bihac municipality, ethnic Bosniaks, and then other ethnicities. Can you just please confirm that all the following lists were processed and produced according to the same methodology, regardless of the fact that they are in relation or about war invalids as opposed to the previous ones?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, all of the ones that we've gone through and all of the ones that we've commented on dealt with members of the HVO who were killed, and now we come to the war invalids of the HVO, and again the information was processed in the same way as in relation to previous lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you look at 2D 00616. Again, war invalids, Bosanski Brod municipality, all ethnicities; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the 101 Bosanski Brod Brigade. Again, a list of all war invalids, Croats, Bosniaks, other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine, move on to the next one. 2D 00617. This is a list of war invalids for Bosanski Samac municipality, all ethnicities; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is a list of war invalids of the HVO, Samac municipality, 104 - that is the number of the Brigade - HVO. Again, this was produced and processed in the same way as the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Next one up is 2D 00168. War invalids from Brcko municipality all ethnicities; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the 108 Brigade of the HVO. Again, listed in the same way as those previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Next one is 2D 00169. War invalids -- 619. Derventa municipality. All ethnicities; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's right. This is 103, the 103 Derventa Brigade of the HVO, and the list was produced to be able to contain all the elements that were contained in previous reports in relation to previous that we've gone through.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Next one up is 2D 620. This is a list of war invalids from Gradacac municipality?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This is the 107th Brigade of the HVO, Gradacac. Again, processed much in the same way as the previous ones. War invalids, Croats, Bosniaks, and other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please move on to 2D 00621.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This is a list of the one -- of five members of the HVO from Modrica municipality, or, rather, members of the 105 Brigade of the HVO, Modrica Brigade. The list was put together in much the same way as all of the previous lists that we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Next one up is 2D 00622.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The list of war invalids of the HVO Odzak municipality, Croats, the 102 Brigade of the HVO. Bosniaks, other ethnicities, members of that municipality who were killed -- or wounded, rather, I do apologise, while the -- serving in other units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The last in this series of documents is 2D 00624, and you are the one who provided these documents for our benefit.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Another HVO document, the 115 Brigade of HVO, Zrinski, Tuzla, processed in the same way as all the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, this completes our overview of documents in relation to those killed as well as war invalids from the Bosanski Posavina zone, which is the zone in which you were active. Let us try to wrap up this story by asking the following question. All of these members, or, rather, their families and war invalids, were looked after equally in the same way based on what you told us regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: All of the HVO members, regardless of their ethnicity, were looked after in the same way and to the same extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please move on to the next document, 2D 00627. This is a document submitted by the federal ministry for combatants and invalids of the homeland war. It is also called the federal ministry for defenders and invalids of the homeland war. The date is the 12th of March, 2008, and I was the one who requested a copy of this document. Can we please just check what the document is about and then you will confirm for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, as long as you can, whether this ministry was the relevant ministry for issuing this sort of information or indicators. This is a list containing the names of the members of the 4th HVO Brigade, the Stjepan Radic Brigade from Ljubuski, these are the ethnic Bosniaks. And it gives you the names, the years of birth, and the time spent in service. The 31st of May, 1992 ending with the 15th of July, 1993. Mr. Buljan, can you please confirm because you, too, were working with the federal bodies, this ministry would have been responsible for issuing information like this?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I think this ministry might have issued information of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please move on to a different document and this is P 4756. This is a meeting of the collegium of Defence Department heads, and it was held on the 2nd of September, 1993. Mr. Buljan, can you please tell the Chamber whether perhaps you attended this meeting of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, I did not attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 5. Have a look please. Specifically item 6. May I just draw your attention to a particular portion pertaining to the welfare structure. So item 6 reads, this is the last sentence of paragraph 2 that I'm about to read back to you.
