"The new organisation scheme for the general care [as interpreted] administration was adopted and the conclusion was reached that the families of those Muslim members of the HVO who were killed should still receive assistance." Judge Antonetti asked you whether you knew what was going on in May, you say you didn't. And I'm asking you based on this document, does it not seem to follow that the families of those Croat members who were killed were looked after -- even after the 2nd of September, 1993? And my other question in relation to this is: Based on your knowledge did the care continue after this? Because you did have all the information, didn't you, once you were in a position to consolidate all this information based on the reports that we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This conclusion shows that the Muslim members as indicated here were looked after up and until this conclusion, and I can assert in no uncertain terms that that the care continued after this conclusion. I don't know what the back drop was for this collegium meeting and what exactly was discussed; however, these were times in Bosnia-Herzegovina when there was a war between Croats and Serbs, between Serbs and Bosniaks, between Bosniaks and Croats, between Bosniaks and Bosniaks. Someone was probably asking themselves what to do in a given situation. But here I'll repeat this, both before and after this, all of the members of the HVO received the same care in the same way and to the same extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you now look, please at 2D 00625, please, and explain to Their Honours what this is?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In my introduction I said that for a certain period of time I was deputy director of the federal administration for questions of veterans and invalids of the homeland war. Therefore, the director, Ivanisevic and myself agreed that for the first time we should sit down and exchange information about the killed, wounded, and missing members so that at the time I had the data regarding members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and for him to be informed about members of the HVO who had been killed and wounded and who were missing. So this was an effort on our part, that is the director and myself, we exchanged data about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to ask you this: The director of the federal administration was Mr. Suad Porusovic [phoen], is he a Bosniak ethnicity I have to ask that you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Bosniak ethnicity. In that period appointments were made in such a way that if the director was a Bosniak, then the deputy would be a Croat and vice-versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you at the beginning and that is my omission, were you ever a member of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: By this protocol, you actually carried out the first exchange of data regarding the members of the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What in fact were the two of you endeavouring to achieve by doing this?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The war had only just ended. We are talking about 1998 -- or recently ended, the war ended with the Dayton Agreements, but on the ground the situation continued tense maybe until mid-1996. And director Porusovic and myself agreed that to begin with we would exchange information so as at least to have the numbers right. How many there were of the various populations so that we could adopt a common approach in relations with the government so that a certain decree or law would be passed to deal in an equal manner with the problems of the victims, members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did that happen, was any such regulation passed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I have to say that I didn't have the good fortune during our term of office for such regulations to be passed. We worked hard on this. We prepared a law. The only difference between the two of us was that I disagreed regarding only two articles of the entire law. I thought that the basis for calculating the assistance to be given for invalids, all invalids in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as for the families of the killed and missing, should be based on the average salaries of the active duty officer. However, my colleague Porusovic did not agree. He thought that the average for the entire Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be used. We prepared such a draft law, we sent it to the government, it was adopted by the government. I can't remember how many votes were in favour, how many against, but when that law came before the parliament of the Federation, the parliament was divided in its views along the same lines as the two of us differed. However, when it was eventually adopted, we were no longer holding those posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, you have another five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have that in mind. I only have one more document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as I can understand you, the problem was the amount that the individuals were entitled to, not who was entitled to this remuneration?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: The problem was not who would be remunerated, the dates were not at issue, the beginning and the end, the extent of welfare assistance was not in question, but simply the basis upon which this remuneration was to be calculated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The last document is 2D 00628, and could you explain to Their Honours what it is?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, we have before us a law on the rights of defenders and members of their families adopted by the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What colleague Porusovic and myself failed to do in 1998 and 1999, the colleagues who took over later, four years later, this law appeared in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina number 33 in the year 2004. And Article number 2 defines what I was speaking about a moment ago and the parliament adopted it and this law was adopted. And after it came into force, it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to the law who is defined as a defender?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Article 2, Article 2 speaks of members of the family, but it all defines the defenders as members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the Croatian Defence Council and of the police force of the relevant Internal Affairs body who participated in the Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The beginning of the aggression, being the 18th of September, 1991, up until the 23rd of December, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the beginning is the date when the municipality of Ravno was attacked; is that right? So this applied to members of the HVO and of the army, and they enjoyed equal rights regardless of whether they were Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This law defined the rights and entitlements of the defenders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to say that on page 50, line 5, I asked you to look at Article 2, and you have read out Article 2 so that this should be quite clear in the transcript; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, I just read Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for your testimony, and that brings to an end my examination-in-chief of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question, a very simple one, to put to you, but it refers to the beginning of your testimony when Madam Nozica asked you what you were doing and you told us that your brigade was facing the Serbs. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am afraid I have not understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the very beginning of your testimony, my understanding was that you said at certain point in time that your brigade was on the frontline confronting the Serbs, is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we didn't have an interpretation, that is why the witness is not able to answer. He didn't get an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard now?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have heard you. The 103rd Derventa Brigade throughout the war was confronting the Serbs and that was the positions we held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the 103rd Brigade, there were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourself and your comrade soldiers, what were you defending facing the Serbs? Were you defending the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were defending Herceg-Bosna, you were defending the territory of Posavina? What were you defending?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the first part of my testimony I said I was born in Kuljanovci which is a locality 5 kilometres from Derventa. On the 8th of April, I was at my work-place, and in the afternoon the Serbian army shelled my village, the village I was born in. From my village almost right up to Banja Luka, there's not a single other Croatian village. That is the only Croatian village there. All of us in the whole army, including Bosniaks, Croats, and all others, we were defending our territory. I wanted to return where I went daily from work. So that was our aim, for the Croats to continue living where they were living before, to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question which has nothing to do with the previous question and it will be my last. We were looking at the documents with the statistics of people killed and wounded, and I have to tell you, I was deeply impressed with the figures I see. There were 780 wounded, thousands of killed, thousands of wounded, therefore I assume that many families were affected by this conflict. Does this create such traumatism today? Does this trauma still exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, certainly after events of this kind and everything that happened, all those who were affected and especially those who lost their loved ones, their fathers, and their children, certainly they are traumatised. Some of them more, some of them less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm looking at D3, D4, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm on my feet for the first, though the Defence of Coric has no question for this witness, but this is our order of appearance so I wish to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Your Honours, we have no questions for the gentleman, and we wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll leave out D2. So D3 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours and everybody in the courtroom. Praljak Defence will have a couple of questions, and when I finish I think that Mr. Praljak would like to raise only one question related to the geography mainly. Perhaps we'll get the maps in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buljan, I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Praljak. We have met and I will have a few questions for you. You told us everything about your activities, the positions you held in the 103rd Brigade and the operation zone at the very beginning of your testimony. Tell me, please, you said that in July 1992, you actually had to leave your positions in Derventa and the surroundings and that you were slowly retreating essentially towards the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that is, towards Bosanski Brod; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. We were retreating towards Bosanski Brod as Bosanski Brod is across the river from Slavonski Brod, that is where we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should explain the geography for Their Honours, which they may not be familiar with. So the entire area of Posavina is the northern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Basically, it is the region along the Sava river, and that is why it is called Posavina, and actually it is a border region bordering on the Republic of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your enemy that you fought, the JNA or the Serbs, were pushing you into that area towards Sava from the southeastern part, from your southeastern part; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were pushed into a narrow area south of the Sava river; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the northern side of the river, though the border doesn't follow strictly the Sava river, but anyway northward in relation to the Sava is the frontier with the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when the Serb offensive is squeezing you into an ever smaller area, you have nowhere to go?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After Derventa fell, the civilians were withdrawing towards Croatia too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in a couple of days in July 1992, a certain number of civilians and a number of soldiers that had abandoned the HVO were on the -- in the meadows east of Bosanski Brod intending to cross the Sava to go to Bosanski Brod and Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea of what the numbers were, are we talking hundreds or thousands?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I think that one could say that there were thousands. I couldn't say whether it was 3.000 or 2.000, but the area where they were sitting during the day and the night, and the command of my brigade was close by too so that I saw those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And those people had nowhere to go; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from Bosanski Brod to Slavonski Brod, and here is says from Bosanski Brod to Bosanski Brod. People were going line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We'll repeat that for the record. People from the surroundings of Bosanski Brod, which means the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wanted to cross the Sava to the north in the direction of Slavonski Brod; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, from the Derventa and from Bosanski Brod, some people had come earlier from Modrica and Odzak, which is the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they gathered there in front of the bridge intending to enter the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why did they assemble there? Why couldn't they cross over into the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: At that time, I don't know why, but I know it was physically impossible to cross over because at the time there were obstacles on the bridge and passage over the bridge was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I have obtained correct information, the Bosnian authorities weren't controlling that border pass, the Croatian authorities wouldn't allow the people to cross over, they controlled the pass; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I think that at that time at that pass there were police forces from Bosanski Brod, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from Croatia, but you know, when you are entering someone else's state then you always ask the police of that state for permission to enter the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. And that when on for a few days because the Croatian authorities wouldn't allow those refugees to cross over into the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: That went on for a few days. I can't say whether it went on for three or four days, but it certainly lasted for a number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then finally the border was opened and the people started crossing over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, at one point in time, the border was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long was necessary, half a day, a day, three days, for those people to cross over? Roughly speaking, I know no one knows the precise answer?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't know how long was needed, but people would simply cross over the bridge, it's fairly quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And they crossed over into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you were in the immediate vicinity at the time, it was naturally a problem because the people were in the field and no care was provided for them. Bosanski Brod was under fire, it was being shelled by Serbian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. This occurred on a daily basis and on a number of occasions. Bosanski Brod and its surroundings were shelled on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we say that those refugees, those people were in fact constantly exposed to danger?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, they were constantly exposed to danger. More so than other people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When they finally started crossing over, since you were there, did you hear anything about how this pass was opened up? Did anyone play a role in this and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In my command amongst the troops there were rumours according to which the person responsible for opening up the pass was General Praljak. I can't confirm that I saw the general down there at the time, but I wasn't there all the time. Our lines were below Bosanski Brod, but I know that such rumours were spread at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there were such information relayed by those people at the time in that narrow stretch of territory?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the following days after those people had already entered the territory of Croatia, did you perhaps hear anything about a certain conflict, a clash of some kind, a clash of various opinions between General Praljak and the authorities in the Republic of Croatia with regard to opening up this pass?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, I think that I can say that there were such rumours, such things were discussed. It was said that certain leading individuals in the Republic of Croatia would take certain punitive measures directed at General Praljak because of what had been done. I can't say that I read about it or saw this on television, but this is what soldiers spoke about amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me reminds you of something. I'd like to provide a time-frame for what we are talking about. Before that exodus and quite a long time before that exodus, Vukovar had already fallen and the Serbian forces had taken a large part of Slavonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time or later on Croatia had a lot of its own refugees?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I know that there were displaced individuals. It was a difficult situation, there was a war, and you have the population moving from certain towns, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As an educated man and someone who was in particular involved in the field of welfare, do you know that Croatia in fact had a huge burden because it had to take care of its own citizens who had been displaced because of the war, and it had to take care of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me something else -- MS. WEST. Objection. Sorry to interrupt. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. I'm just -- a couple of comments here. First and foremost I've let this -- I've not commented on this, but this is beyond the scope of cross-examination. Secondly, it's unclear to me how this would be relevant to our indictment. And thirdly, if you are inclined to let it continue, I would ask that it not be leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak -- I apologise, Mr. Kovacic, before you continue to discuss this subject, I'd like to suggest to my colleagues that we withdraw or deduct certain time from the time allocated to you, because these aren't questions that arose in the course of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can respond to what my colleague said. It's quite clear that my subject relates to testimony of this witness. I went beyond the scope only when I tried to give a time-frame for the event. I tried to refer to parallel events, to the situation in Croatia at the time that these refugees arrived. So this was just a reference. This was just a context I wanted to provide. If you want to deduct that time from me, I'm in your hands, but I think that it's necessary for me to link up certain events to the situation on the ground. If you're not interested in that, I won't explore this any further and I didn't intend to do so in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, when those people crossed the bridge to enter Croatia, et cetera, I think we said that there were some soldiers who had fled the lines, were falling or had fallen, and some soldiers fled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't think there were military able soldiers in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. The Croatian authorities at the border, did they ask those who were armed to disarm?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they didn't allow people who were carrying weapons to enter Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In fact, they first had to disarm and then they let them in?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are some questions about the territory, or perhaps I should allow Mr. Praljak to address this issue. It's a military issue, and I would like to ask the Chamber to allow Mr. Praljak to ask the witness a few questions about the military situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if it concerns military issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On the whole these are military issues. Unfortunately, I asked for a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina but we won't have time, but could the witness be provided with a piece of paper and then we will draw it. I would just like to clarify certain issues. For example, where the territory of Posavina is actually located in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which six brigades were in the part facing Croatia. Cross-examination by Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give the witness a sheet of paper and, Witness, could you explain for the benefit of the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I am sorry for my interruption, but we do have a map available on sanction and General Praljak could use it. On e-court, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the number so that we can pull it up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P 09276. It will just take a moment to get on the screen. And that's map 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be provide with a marker, please. Please, could you first mark the areas or the area where the six HVO brigades, were the 101st, 102nd, 103rd, 104th, the 105th and the 106th Brigade. Could we have a clear copy of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a map on the screen, Witness, and you can use this marker to mark the map. You can use the marker on the screen. The equipment is very good here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the previous map, a clear or clean version of the map, the previous map, number 3. We had it on the screen a moment ago. There was a different version, a clean version of this map before. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please show the area defended, the area facing Croatia so I'm talking about Posavina and the six brigades. It doesn't have to be precise, but could you just mark the area?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: If we are talking about the time -- or, rather, the time-period after November 1992 when the brigades were located there in these places, municipalities that fell, well, then the situation would be as follows: Odzak fell --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the fall. So around the municipality of Derventa, that's where the line would go, then this part near Modrica, this just above Gradacac, and the line would continue in this way, Brcko would remain to the right. It's not precisely drawn on the map, but this is what it would like look like more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there six HVO brigades in that area as you said?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, in this area there were six HVO brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Serbs had a corridor, and on the other side of the corridor there was Tuzla and the 115th HVO Brigade and the 107th HVO Brigade. Could you mark that, too, in a rough manner. It doesn't have to be precise on the map.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: So this is what it would look like more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was a narrow corridor, and the Serbian forces tried to enlarge the corridor as it was important, it was a corridor in the vicinity of Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And my last question, since no one asked you whether you knew I was there or not, was it a bloody war, a bloody conflict? Were there many casualty, many wounded, many dead? Were there huge losses among HVO fighters, suffered by HVO fighters?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: From the beginning to the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- from the end -- from the beginning to the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina I was there, but I have to admit that the situation was the worst in Bosanska Posavina. If you have a look at the territory from east, from west, from all directions it's possible from tanks to pass through. Often one would say we had everything, we experienced everything, but we didn't have parachutists attacking us, but we experienced everything else, tank attacks, plane attacks, and so on and so forth. It was terrible here. It's a small area and there were a lot of people who were killed, a lot of wounded. My unit was in Derventa. And if we have a look at the map, not at any point in time did I launch an attack. I was on the defensive all the time. The troops withdrew all the time in this direction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that only your brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the accused's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 103rd HVO Brigade had over 400 members who were killed, and that also concerns the 101st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the difference when it came to equipment? What did you use to defend yourselves and against what did you have to defend yourselves?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps when the time comes, when I get over all of it, perhaps I'll write something about this. But the biggest chapter will have to do with the lack of ammunition, ammunition for light weapons and also for heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank the Judges, the Prosecution, and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like us to give the document an IC number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned IC number 917. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Alaburic, will you conclude?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good day, good day to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, good day to you too. I will have a few very brief questions. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that you have a lot of documents. Have others given you some time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I don't think I'll need a lot of time. I think that we'll conclude in 15 minutes time. It all depends on the witness's answers. But we can now distribute the documents that we have. While doing this, and perhaps the usher could hand the documents out. We weren't sure whether we would have time to commence in the course of this hearing, that's why we haven't handed them out already.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, this is also an explanation for the Trial Chamber. I would like to show you a document indicating the number of Muslims in your brigade. Therefore, could you please shed some light on that, confirm or correct in as far as there are any corrections that need making. Then I would like to ask you a couple of questions with today's evidence, especially as it related to assistant commanders of brigades and operations areas. Security assistants, health assistants, morale assistants. I will be showing you a number of documents in relation to that as well. I don't necessarily think you said anything that needs correcting, but I think it might be helpful for the Trial Chamber to get more of an insight into the who the brigade commanders were, how they were appointed, and the way the whole thing was organised. Therefore, if there's anything you can tell us about that, our conversation might prove to be a little lengthier than I first thought. You have a set of documents before you, sir, they are in arithmetic order. This is not necessarily the order which I will be following. I may decide to skip the occasional document, depending on what you tell us. The first document that I want you to look at is D 3355 -- P. It's Prosecution document. P 3355. This is a report on the work of the Defence Department relating to the period between January and June 1993, page 11 of the Croatian. The English reference, I'm giving the figure in the upper right corner, 9094.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you got the document, sir? This is something about Derventa Brigade, the 103 Brigade, which at the time the report was produced which was at the -- early in July 1993 received some men, 161 military conscripts, 59 of whom were Croats. Or rather, 539 of whom were Croats. A total of 861 men, 8-6-1 military conscripts, 539 Croats, that is the breakdown, 308 Muslims, and 14 Serbs. Based on your recollection, Mr. Buljan, would that tally with your information concerning the ethnic structure of the Derventa Brigade in mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I think it does roughly. I'm not going into the nitty-gritty, but that would be it roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next sentence is particularly interesting. It might be of interest to the Chamber because they hear about the existence of six brigades in Bosanski Posavina and a lot of other brigades throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, can you please comment on the following sentence, it reads: "This -- the required strength in manpower is 3.096 conscripts." That's what it says. Mr. Buljan, does that not mean that in terms of its establishment, the brigade was supposed to have 3.096 men, soldiers, but in actual fact all it had at the time was 861 men?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: It is quite obvious that the establishment-wise the brigade like this needed 3.096 conscripts or men, all they had was the figure you specified.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So when we talk about an HVO brigade in these terms, it doesn't necessarily always mean that the actual number of men reflected the one envisaged in a brigade's establishment; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: If there's a rule to be deduced from all of this, then the rule would be that none of the HVO brigades were up to their full manning levels. The manning levels that they were supposed to have establishment-wise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. And now several questions about the assistant commanders of these brigades. You told us that the commanders of brigades and operations areas have certain assistants that helped them with certain work areas, morale, health, security, that sort of thing; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you now please tell us, if you know, how this was regulated, who had the right to appoint these men? Who had the right to dismiss them, these assistant brigade commanders and assistant commanders of operation zones?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't think I can be very specific about the procedure itself, how these men were appointed, but I can tell you how I was appointed to the position of assistant commander of IPD.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is what I propose: Let's look at the regulations first and then we'll see whether that was how it worked in practice in your brigade. I do wish to point out any differences to the Chamber between a de jure situation and a de facto situation. Can you please look at 2D 567. This is a decision of internal structure of the Defence Department and the date is October 1992. Can you please look at item D. We'll be dwelling on the morale because you probably happen to know more about that than anything else. Item D sub-item (6) can you please look at paragraph 2, I'm about to read it out to you: "Assistant commanders of morale of the south-east Herzegovina operations area of the north-west Herzegovina operations area of the central Bosnia operations area and the Bosnian Posavina operations area, assistant commander for morale of the Bruno Busic independent regiment, assistant commanders for morale of the special purpose unit, and assistant brigade commanders for morale are appointed by the head of the Defence Department at the proposal of assistant head for morale." Mr. Buljan, did you know that this was the procedure envisaged by the regulations?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: When all of this was going on back in 1992, in October, November, possibly September, I was not aware of this procedure, nor indeed was I aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your reply I conclude that you found out about this later on, is that not the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, at any rate, later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us about how you were appointed to your position as assistant commander for morale?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: When large tracts of the territory were lost and two-thirds of the command staff were dismissed for various reasons, or were out of action for various reasons, because they were wounded or because they left, the brigade commander simply told me, As of today, you shall be my assistant for IPD. Soon there will be a procedure in progress to obtain all the right documents for you. He was loud and clear about my task and how I should go about coming to grips with my task.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, these assistant commanders for morale -- brigades, morale commanders of brigade -- brigades and operations areas, are they the part of the Defence Department of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I really can't answer that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. There's another detail that I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber because I think they might find it extremely helpful in order to come to grips with the question I'm about to ask you. Can you please go to document P 646. This is a proposal for the work programme of the Defence Department up and until the end of 1992. If you go to each chapter entitled "Morale," this is page 3, could you look at the second sentence, saying that: "It is necessary to establish both vertical and horizontal links, coordination, and hierarchy." Mr. Buljan, could you perhaps shed light for our benefit on what the horizontal links might be and what the vertical links might be?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I have to say that I've never seen this before. And I can't shed light on this. Vertical links, horizontal links, that should be clear enough in itself shouldn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you find it that clear, can you please share that with us. I assume it might be helpful for the Chamber to have an explanation on what these horizontal and vertical links might be?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I didn't mean in this specific instance. I meant quite generally. Horizontal and vertical. I didn't read this carefully and this wasn't the sort of subject matter that I was dealing with at the time. Therefore, I can hardly be expected to provide a reliable answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll show you a diagram. Perhaps it will help us along, being that we are trying to find some sort of an answer. The diagram is 2D 685. This is a diagram or a chart of the Morale Sector of the Herceg-Bosna Defence Department. This is a Bruno Stojic Defence document. Can you please have a look. The document shows certain military units from the battalion level and platoon level to the operation zones, and you can see that there are assistant commanders for morale throughout. And now with see these links from the operation zone to the assistant head for morale. Can you have a look at the chart, please, and tell us if the chart is consistent with your knowledge on how the Morale Sector was organised?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I really can't say anything about this. I only dealt with this very briefly, and then I moved on to something entirely different. I was also physically distant from where all of this was going on, so with all due respect, I cannot contribute anything meaningful to this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the nature of the witness's answers in this respect I have no further question Norris witness and, Mr. Buljan, I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I didn't wish to interrupt Ms. Alaburic when she asked you about the procedure for your appointment. As assistant commander for morale, I'm looking at page 68 in the transcript, lines 10 and onwards. You answered a question. You said that the brigade commander one fine day told you, From today on you shall be assistant for morale. My question to you is the following: How did the appointment take place in practice? How were brigade commanders appointed and their assistants, too? I want to know particularly about your case, your appointment as assistant commander. I'm not sure if this translates well. We have a commander or a brigade commander, was he the one making the appointment or was the appointment actually made by a department head or perhaps the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when all of this was going on, the situation was an extremely difficult one in the area in which this was happening, and these were difficult times as well. The war had already been in full swing for a very long time. The army in a way began to sit on its hands and became onlookers, mere onlookers. Derventa had fallen and most of the command staff had been replaced. Given the situation, the commander believed that I could give him a hand in all of this at the time, and he said you shall be my assistant for IPD. The documents will soon be on their way. I was now given a mission and was told specifically what I should do, how I should go about my work, and how I should go about reporting whack back to him. All of this was something that we had to do in our stride. It wasn't like we were sitting around in offices using typewriters or anything like that. We had to think on our feet and do things as we kept moving along, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So the documents were soon to be on their way. And who was to issue these documents to back your appointment? Which authority and whose signature would they bear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't reply right now. I didn't analyse that, I didn't look into that, and I didn't mind that too much. My job was welfare, and I devoted all of my energy in those years to that particular area. Therefore, the IPD itself was a passing adventure for me. Perhaps not an adventure but it only covered for me a brief period of time that I spent working there. I specified this in my CV. It's as simple as that. It was a very brief period. No more than two months, two and a half months perhaps. I didn't look much into that to be quite honest. Therefore, I can't say exactly what the correct procedure would have been. If I were given a chance to go through the documents I'd probably arrive at some conclusion or other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 minute break and then the Prosecutor will commence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecutor, let us discuss our schedule. As you know next week we have nothing scheduled for Wednesday because there should be a 7th or an 8th trial in progress. However, that slot has been freed up now, so we believe that if necessary we can plough on from Monday to Thursday. If we conclude on Wednesday, then the Thursday will be off. But we will sit on Wednesday. I now give the floor to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Kim West. I'm with the Office of the Prosecution, and I'm just going to ask you some questions at least until 7.00 this evening. I think it might be helpful that the first place we go to is the maps that we looked at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I can have P 09276 on e-court, and that's map 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Where is the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Map 3 is in the bottom left-hand corner. But do you see map in front of you that says "The Croatian Communities of Herceg-Bosna and Bosanski Posavina 1991"?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, specifically, I understand that you were born at least close to Derventa, which is up in the Posavina, and for the record that's the area in the north eastern section of Bosnia. Do you see that on the map, it's coloured in blue?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Derventa is not a part of the Community of Herceg-Bosna, is it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: This map reflects the situation in 1991. At the time Derventa had the same status as all the other municipalities in Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so my question at least during the period of time in 1991, Derventa, would you agree with me, is not part of the Herceg-Bosna community?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether the division was like this in 1991. Back in 1991 Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have the blue coloured areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me remind you of the question that Judge Antonetti asked you earlier today, and he asked you: When you, in 1992, were fighting with the HVO, what were you defending. And do you remember your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Against the Serbs. There is obviously an error, an interpretation error. They were fighting with the HVO, but in French there was an interpretation problem. Can you please restate your question, madam, in order to clarify this whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question, sir, was in 1992 when you were fighting for the HVO, what were you defending?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I do apologise to the learned friend. The interpretation that we are receiving and the witness is my friend is asking in 1991. The witness was, in fact, not speaking about 1991. Not at all. The transcript reflects 1992. Now, we are not entirely clear as to what my learned friend is asking about, 1991 or 1992, because back in 1991 there was nothing that the witness mentioned, and I think that is why the witness now nonplussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So my question regards 1992. I understand that you started in the HVO in 1992. So in 1992, what were you defending?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: As you said, I'm a native of Derventa municipality. Derventa had a total of 52 villages. There was the town, too, Derventa itself. The villages were mixed, some were Serb and some were Croat. At this time the situation that arose was this: The Serbs would attack the Croats in Derventa municipality in order to take their positions. This happened on the 8th of April, 1992, where I lived. From that moment on, members of the 103rd Derventa Brigade and the HVO never took another step forward into anyone else's village, area, or town. We just kept defending our own area in which we were living at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, and you just indicated that the Serbs were attacking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a problem because the English translation reads: "... members of the 103rd Derventa Brigade and the HVO." Is this the HVO or is this the members of the 103rd Derventa Brigade and the HVO, what exactly did you say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said those were members of the 103rd Derventa Brigade of the HVO, or the HVO. So it would be 103rd, that was its name, it was part of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, your enemy was the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can turn to map 7, map 7 of this same exhibit, 09276.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a map showing the Serb autonomous areas or the areas in which the Serbs believed to be their own. Would you agree with me that Derventa is within the Serb -- an area in which the Serbs believe to be theirs?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't know. According to the 1991 census, Derventa had about 22.000 Serb, about 21.000 Croats, 98 Croats less than the Serbs, and about 7.000 or 8.000 Bosniaks or perhaps slightly more. This map, the way it looks with the area marked in green, in terms of the Serbs not being interested in the area or that indeed it really was like this, that this was the physical reality, if that had been the case, I'm sure the clashes would never have erupted in Derventa itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Mr. Buljan, you would agree with me that the Serbs were interested in your area and that's why they were your enemy?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you also agree in looking at this map, it appears that the Serbs did not -- did not want a substantial portion of Herceg-Bosna as their own? A substantial portion of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I don't know if that was the case or not. If they wanted that or not. It was a long war and a war of attrition, it lasted from 1992 until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, if you can go to the first binder. The first Prosecution binder. And take a look at P 09551. And the B/C/S is in the back, but before we start speaking about that document let me just ask you a few questions. There you go. Now, just to go over your background. Up until April of 1995 you were the head of welfare for Posavina; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But then in April of 1995 your job changed, and you became the head of the HR H-B administration of welfare within the Ministry of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you physically move to Mostar when you were appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In 1995 the road was not exactly open for normal traffic yet. If one wanted to get from Moradze [phoen] to Mostar across Bosnia-Herzegovina, one needed to make a detour via the Republic of Croatia the long way around passing through Biljovar-Zagreb [phoen] and so on and so forth. I was on my own, so it was only logical for me to move, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the answer to that is yes; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you've spoken briefly about the fact that when you arrived in this position, you consolidated the data that had been taken in by the welfare departments and you created various reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: There wasn't too much consolidation going on. I think I just hurried certain processes along in order to get the implementation off the ground as quickly as possible in order to reach lasting solutions in order to help invalids and casualties of the homeland war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But in this position as now the head of welfare for the whole republic, you had access to data that was beyond the Posavina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if you look at P 09551, and we are going to look at page 6 of the English, and for you it's page 5 in the B/C/S, and it's the red tab that you see on top. I'm just going to read part of this and then ask you a question. This document talks about the activities of the welfare department during the period of time from July to December of 1993 when you were the head of the republic's department. And it says that: "Among other things, the following activities were carried out," and we are talking about the welfare department, "coordination and control of the welfare departments, the military districts, to who whom professional assistance was also provided, oversight of the course of treatment and medical rehabilitation of wounded members and hospitals, sanatoria and rehabilitation centres, analysis of the results of diagnostic procedures related to the type, category, and grade of physical disability of invalids of the homeland war, preparation of drafts, legal proposals, projects and programs related to solving the entire welfare problems of the sufferers, cooperation with institutions and other organisations in the interest of solving those problems, and ensuring of financial means for the realisation of one off and long term rights of the sufferers, and determining the priority order. And keeping of unique computerised records for all killed, missing, imprisoned, wounded, and sick members of the HVO and members of their families. "Cooperation with emigres, hospitals from abroad, charity organisations, societies and institutions in regard with the assistance to the wounded and killed members of their families and supervision of managing graves and graveyards where the killed members of the HVO were buried." Mr. Buljan, would you agree with me -- or, rather, is this list that I just read out consistent with what you were responsible for as the head of the welfare department for the republic?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes. More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And specifically I'm going to focus your attention on the language here having to do with computers. It says "... keeping of unique computerised records for all killed, missing, imprisoned, wounded and sick members of the HVO and their families." This computer system of which it speaks, was that something that you worked with when you became head of the welfare department in April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, we complemented these lists and each war disabled person who had disability had to go to a second level commission. He had to have a written decision and certification of his invalidity. And this is a list that was done then. I was engaged in this and -- and this was -- this is continuing to this day to establish whether somebody was indeed a member and whether he was indeed a wounded in the way he was. The law defines this and the times such as they are. Sometimes we have documents that are not complete and that is why some of those documents are being revised and activities are ongoing to complement these lists if necessary and amend them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And these lists that were on the computer, would you agree with me that they would include lists of HVO soldiers in say Mostar and Stolac in those areas within the Herceg-Bosna community?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: There's no reason for them not to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was the computer system unable to separate those HVO soldiers who were Muslim from those HVO soldiers who were Croats in?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, the computer did not have such a programme to indicate that, but records were simply kept by the names, the first and last name, their registration number, when they were killed, when they were detained, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so you and your department made determinations as to which soldiers were Croat and which soldiers were Muslims based on names; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I can't say that it is possible to determine in each and every case, but in principle when you read out a name, one can assume what the ethnicity is, but it need not necessarily be so each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. West, I'm sorry, you combined up two questions. One was whether at all they made a distinction between Muslims and Croats. I don't think that was said before. And then you said, on what basis. So I think the foundation was missing for your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back and rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, on direct examination you spoke about your own brigade, the 103rd in Derventa. And in that brigade you actually showed us a record, and I think it was 2D 00150, that spoke about and gave figures of how many Croats were in that brigade and others and how many Muslims were in that brigade and others. Do you have any understanding as to how 2D 00150 was made? It's not going to be in your file. It was an exhibit that you looked at during your direct testimony. There you go.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: First of all, these data about the 101st to the 106th Brigade, I must say that they more or less correspond to my knowledge about it. Now, whether it's exactly 31.45, but 28 is certainly a good approximation. This is regarding these records. As for the person who signed this, then that person could sign it, and I consider this document to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll of move on. In 1995, April of 1995, when you became the head of the welfare department for the republic, you've indicated that you became familiar with information that was beyond the Posavina. So I'd like to talk about some of the areas that are outside the Posavina. So, for example, the first area I would like to talk about is -- or the first brigade I would like to talk about is the 3rd Brigade. Can you look at P 10797.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question hasn't been put to the witness, but I do wish to object for the record. This again is a new document, and the Defence will object every time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that, very well, but the Chamber by a majority vote has decided to allow the Prosecutor to touch upon subjects that were not covered in the examination-in-chief. This is not my opinion, but the majority opinion. We will stop there, that's clear. A decision has been rendered. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, apologise, I also wish for the record to say that the Defence for General Petkovic joins Mr. Stojic's Defence objection, and I think that we should be guided by the decision of this trial from November, and I think that should apply to each new document, and we will be objecting each time because this is contrary to the decision of the Trial Chamber from November 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, if a document was not on the 65 ter list, if you use it, it's only for the purpose of the credibility of the witness. Have you understood my remark?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do understand your remark and I understand the ongoing discussion on this particular issue. It's our position, as has already been repeated, that we don't believe it needs to be on the 65 ter list. At this point the document that I'm going to be using not only goes to the credibility of the witness but also goes to the direct opposition of what he has testified in front of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in front of you, 10797, are payroll records dated January 1994 for the 3rd Brigade. And these are soldiers in the 3rd Brigade that served various times from 1991 and 1994. I know that you've -- is it true that you've never seen these documents before?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: No, I've never seen them before.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, for the purposes of this question, I'm going to tell you that there's 1.795 soldiers listed. And I'm also going to tell you that it appears that there are 26 soldiers who appear to have Muslim names. Now, just assuming for the purpose of this question that that number 26 is correct, would you agree that the percentage of Muslims in the 3rd Brigade is a much less percentage than the Muslims in the Posavina brigades?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to object. The document which my learned friend has just shown to the witness is dated the 20th of January, 1994. The witness spoke about documents which were prepared before the 30th of June, 1993. Everyone in this courtroom knows that on the 30th of June there was a drastic change in relationship between the Croats and Muslims in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, so I think my learned friend is now trying to compare periods, time periods which are completely incomparable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood and I'll explain to the Prosecutor who I'm sure has understood. Madam Prosecutor, when the Defence showed documents about the composition of the 103rd Brigade, and there were a large number of Muslims, and the document you're showing is from 1994. In the mean time an event took place in the month of June, which could explain the reduction of the number of effectives, we agree don't we? So please put your question within that framework. Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly, I think that there must be some confusion. The witness spoke about the 103rd Brigade, and the -- Madam Prosecutor has asked about the 3rd Brigade. These are two different brigades in two different areas. Secondly, could my learned friend tell us - because I can't see from this document - which is the source and what is the author of this document, and how does she come to the conclusion that it is a payroll list? Because I can see that -- can't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Prosecutor. The witness comes from the 103rd Brigade, not the 3rd Brigade. I thought of this, but I thought maybe it was a slip of the tongue, that she meant 103rd. But we have to see, if we are talking about the 3rd Brigade it has nothing to do with 103rd Brigade. We must agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's not a slip of the tongue. I understand that this is the 3rd Brigade in Mostar, but the witness has already testified that in April of 1995 he became the head of the welfare department for the republic, and as a result of the computerized system he had access to all those HVO soldiers in all of Herceg-Bosna, which is the reason I'm now asking him about soldiers outside the Posavina. In addition, I'm aware of the event in Mostar on June 30th, and as Ms. Alaburic has indicated that would make a significant difference in the number of Muslims, and we are going to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you wish to put a question about the 3rd Brigade in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before that question is posed, I wish to draw attention to another detail. As Madam Alaburic says, this is the documents of the 28th of January, 1994. My learned friend says that the witness in mid-1995 took over this position and could have insight into these documents. But we are talking about different periods. This is a year and a half before. There must -- a basis must be established. When you joined that office in 1995, did you see all the data from the past or from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... explain that. The witness, and the record will reveal itself, spoke about joining the welfare department for the republic in April of 1995. And his first job there was consolidating data from 1992 onwards, so this person would have the ability to talk about earlier HVO soldiers. But it -- may I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please continue. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, you've heard this discussion, are you aware of an event on June 30th, 1993, in Mostar in which the ABiH attacked the northern barracks in Mostar? Are you aware of that event?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I heard about this. At the time I was at the front in Posavina. As for this list, I never told Their Honours that I had all the data about all members of the HVO. All I'm saying is about the killed, war disabled, and families of the killed and missing members of the HVO. I never had a single list of members of the HVO who were not killed or had any disability. So this is a list of all HVO members. I never had any such list in my possession, before or later in my database.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, if you can go to P 07433. I believe it's in the same binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to draw attention that in the e-court, there's an indication that it was not adopted. It was tendered by the Prosecution, but it was not adopted as a document. As an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat the number of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the court officer why this document was not admitted. There are thousands of documents, and I can't respond straightaway. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, you have that in front of you? This is the annual analysis of the performance of the Mostar defence administration in 1993. And if we go to the introduction which is page 3 of English, it's also page 3 of the B/C/S. This memo talks about the 1993 analysis or review of the defence administration, and it talks about those offices under it, the work that they did, the difficulties that they encountered, and then what sort of solutions they could have to overcome them. But I would like you to go in this to page 6 of the B/C/S, and that's page 5 of the English. And that page is entitled: "Overview of Conscripts Engaged in Combat in the Mostar Municipality and Their Percentage in Relation to the Number of Military Conscripts VO in Military Records." Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in this chart it starts with the number of Croat inhabitants, according to the 1991 census, and then it goes on to talk about the conscripts, and it gives different figures with the conscripts. And then finally towards the bottom it goes to the actual brigades. Sir, I'm going to have you look at one more page before I ask you a question because I think it will make more sense. If you could go to page 14 of the B/C/S and that's page 10 of the English. And again, this is the same sort of chart. However this just has to do with Citluk. It says the overview of conscripts engaged in combat in Citluk municipality. And again -- and we have a repeat, it's the number of Croat -- Croat inhabitants, according to the census, and then we have a breakdown from that figure to the number of conscripts. For the purposes of this question, this document goes on and there are further overviews for Siroki Brijeg and Kludo [phoen] and Ljubuski. I mean, to each one of them it's the same type of overview. Would you agree with me that looking at the overview, it does not account for Muslim soldiers; like, for example, the Mostar municipality or the Citluk municipality?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Yes, from this overview one can see that. I haven't seen this list before. It comes from a period when I wasn't there. I didn't need to see it afterwards either, but when I read it I see that the analysis was done in this way as is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, even though you've not seen this before, would you agree with me that the absence of Muslim numbers might be because there's no appreciable number of Muslim HVO soldiers in those units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have a serious objection, and I wouldn't otherwise object. But if the Prosecution is trying to impose that for example in Citluk there are no Muslim soldiers in HVO, then before that there should be a question about national structure in municipality of Citluk. There cannot be Muslim, that's the problem. It's the same as they would ask whether there were Serbs in, I don't know, north pole. There are none. So they cannot participate. Or Greeks in Citluk. Michael told me that there are no Greeks in Citluk. So first that should be established. If there are no Muslim inhabitants, they cannot be represented in HVO. Obviously. This is misleading, this is trick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, before asking the question you had to ask the witness about the composition of the population in Citluk. You could have said there were so many Muslims, so many Croats, and how come there were no Muslim soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that the Chamber has heard demographic information on all these municipality which is the reason I didn't go into it with all this particular witness, but I think that since this witness has indicated that he has not looked at this document I'll move on from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- or Mr. Buljan, you've spoken extensively about the situation in the Posavina, and is it fair to say that throughout the war the relationships between Muslims and Croats in the Posavina was very different than the relationship between Muslims and Croats in Herceg-Bosna or specifically Mostar in the latter half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: We could say that it was different. That in a certain sense it was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber why it was different? Why do you think it was different?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: In Posavina, I've already told you what sort of events unfolded. I've told you about when all these events occurred. As far as Mostar itself is concerned, I have to repeat that throughout that entire period I was present in Bosanska Posavina. I wasn't in Mostar. So reference was made to that incident that occurred in mid-1993. So it's as of that time that certain situations were somewhat different in comparison to the situation in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And so my question is you say that it was different, and I understand that you were in the Posavina and not in, for example, Mostar, but as a person who worked in the HVO, even in Posavina in 1993, didn't you have a sense of what was going on in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent. Mostar wasn't my main concern. I didn't have any -- anything particular to analyse with respect to Mostar. At the time there was a problem throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Bosanska Posavina there was a war against the Serbs. In other areas there was a war against the Bosniaks. In other areas there were Bosniaks fighting Bosniaks. The situation was chaotic. Wherever one found oneself, all one tried to do was to keep as much territory as possible at the time and to sustain minimum losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you will agree with me then that you knew in Mostar, at least in the latter half of 1993, the Croats were fighting the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: I heard that there were such problems down there. I can't agree with you that I knew about that, that it happened in one way or another. It was quite simply a huge area and information wasn't relayed adequately. I was involved in all my work, I was performing all the duties that I had to perform. I didn't follow the situation you are referring to, so I couldn't fully answer your question. Anything else I might say would just amount to speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, forgive me if we push a little bit harder on this. You have already testified that you knew the situation between the Muslims and the Croats was different in Mostar than it was in Posavina. Is that difference because the Muslims and the Croats were fighting each other whereas in the Posavina the Muslims and the Croats were cooperating with each other?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN
utterances.text: Well, that was probably the case. In Posavina the situation was such as it was. I have described it. And in Mostar, as of the time of that incident, there was a certain amount of tension. So in a certain sense, that would be the reason for the differences between the situation in Posavina and Mostar. But at the time, as I have said, Mostar wasn't a particular concern of mine. I didn't analyse it. Mostar is of a 1.000 kilometres away from where I was. That was the case at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buljan, but let's continue to talk about that tension, and you recognise that you understood there were some events going on in Mostar in June of 1993, that you at least knew a bit about. Sir, if you can go to P 02223. It's in the binder in front of you. This is a command post -- well, it's a report from Ljubuski, and Ljubuski is one of the areas that you spoke about in your direct. It's a safety report, and I'll just read the beginning. "The safety situation of the territory covered by the 4th Brigade HVO is a complex regarding the events and conflicts that have been taking place with the Muslim and BiH Army. In the area of Ljubuski municipality, there are about 5.5 percentage inhabitants of the Muslim nationality, and an additional number of 1.000 Muslim refugees. At the territory of Citluk municipality, there's 1.5 per cent Muslims and about 250 refugees. The brigade includes 4.5 Muslim soldiers. Appraising a safety situation, and aggravated relations with the BiH Army at the territory of Mostar municipality, and considering the mentioned 4.5 soldiers, which are with the weapons, military equipment, uniforms, and HVO ID cards, most likely some of them will try to defend the interests of Muslim people. According to received information, some groups and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the sake of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies.
